summary: The most authoritative collection of hadith in Sunni Islam, compiled by Imam Muhammad ibn Ismail al-Bukhari after decades of rigorous scrutiny. Universally regarded as the soundest book after the Quran.
intro_paragraph:
Sahih al-Bukhari stands as the most celebrated and rigorously verified hadith collection in the Islamic tradition. Its compiler, Muhammad ibn Ismail al-Bukhari (194–256 AH / 810–870 CE), devoted over sixteen years to gathering, scrutinizing, and selecting narrations from a corpus he estimated at around 600,000. Only those meeting his exacting standards for chain integrity and narrator reliability were retained — a process he famously performed with ritual purity, offering two units of prayer before recording each hadith.

Al-Bukhari's methodology was built on two foundations: the continuous, unbroken chain of transmission (isnad muttasil) and the highest standard of narrator trustworthiness (thiqa). He required that narrators in a chain not merely be contemporaries but demonstrably likely to have met — a criterion stricter than that applied by his contemporaries. He further tested narrators personally, sometimes traveling weeks to verify a single report.

The collection is structured into ninety-seven books (kutub), subdivided into chapters (abwab) that serve a secondary legal function: al-Bukhari's chapter headings (tarajim al-abwab) are themselves a form of jurisprudential commentary, often quoting a Quranic verse, posing a legal question, or using a slightly variant phrasing to signal a subtle ruling. Scholars have long said that understanding these chapter titles is an independent science — Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani dedicated his landmark twenty-volume commentary Fath al-Bari almost as much to unlocking these headings as to explaining the hadiths themselves.

Reception across the Muslim world has been extraordinary. Al-Bukhari's teacher Ishaq ibn Rahawayh reportedly said upon hearing selections from it that nothing like it had been compiled. The collection became a cornerstone of Islamic legal reasoning, theological argument, and devotional recitation (khatm al-Bukhari) across madrasas and scholarly circles from Khurasan to West Africa. The canonical printed edition most widely used today is based on the recension of al-Firabri, the last surviving student who heard the whole work directly from al-Bukhari.
scope: Covers all major domains of Islamic practice and theology: purification, prayer, fasting, zakat, hajj, trade, marriage and divorce, inheritance, criminal law, jihad, virtues of the Companions, exegesis (tafsir), prophetic biography (sira), manners and etiquette, medicine, and eschatology.
criteria: Highest sahih threshold: unbroken chain with demonstrable contact between each pair of narrators; all narrators fully trustworthy (thiqa) and of sound memory (dabt); no shadh (anomaly) or 'illa (hidden defect). Al-Bukhari's standard is generally considered the most stringent applied to any collection.
